etymology: Webster 1828 treats TOGETHER as adverb: in company; in or into union; in the same place; in the same time; in concert; into junction or a state of union (to sew, knit, pin, or mix things together); and together with as in union or mixture with. This page fills the KJV-gap adverb of gathering. Companion pages already treat assemble, congregation, and church.
biblical_def: Together in Scripture is not a brand and not a vibe. It names what God gathers, what rebels plot, and what Christ actually joins. Genesis will not let the waters stay a chaos: Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place (Gen 1:9). The nations will not let their counsel be private: the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed (Psa 2:2). The Lord will not let the church wait for a crowd: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them (Matt 18:20). Providence will not be a slogan for the uncalled: all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose (Rom 8:28). Union with Christ is not a feeling: hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph 2:6). The dictionary therefore keeps together from becoming either a marketing word for community or a conspiracy that outvotes the Anointed. It is the Bible’s way of saying: gathered by the Lord — or gathered against Him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TOGETHER as in company; in or into union; in the same place or time; in concert; into junction; and together with, in union or mixture with.
webster_full: TOGETH'ER, adverb
1. In company. We walked together to the wood.
2. In or into union. The king joined humanity and policy together.
3. In the same place; as, to live together in one house.
4. In the same time; as, to live together in the same age.
5. In concert; as, the allies made war upon France together.
6. Into junction or a state of union; as, to sew, knit, pin or fasten two things together; to mix things together.
Together with, in union with; in company or mixture with. Take the bad together with the good.
scriptures: Genesis 1:9
And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so.
Psalm 2:2
The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed, saying,
Matthew 18:20
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Romans 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Ephesians 2:6
And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: Together is corrupted when gathering is treated as a brand, when all things work together is stripped of calling, and when counsel against the LORD is baptized as community.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is community-as-product. Matthew 18:20 is two or three gathered in my name, with Christ in the midst. Attractional religion keeps the adverb and drops the Name. A crowd in a room is not the church. The recovery is the presence of the Lord, not the size of the room.

The second corruption is Romans 8:28 as a refrigerator magnet. All things work together for good is promised to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. Therapeutic talk hands the line to the uncalled and calls it the universe. Providence is particular. It is not karma with a cross.

The third corruption is Psalm 2:2 inverted. Kings and rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed. Solidarity is not righteousness. A coalition against Christ is still rebellion, however united. Genesis 1:9 remains the pattern: the Lord gathers; the creature does not get to rename the gathering.
roots_summary: Webster: in company / in union / in concert. usage: The waters are gathered together by decree, not by mood (Gen 1:9).
Rulers take counsel together against the LORD and His Anointed (Psa 2:2); two or three gathered together in my name have Christ in the midst (Matt 18:20).
All things work together for good to the called (Rom 8:28); the saints are raised and seated together in Christ (Eph 2:6).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats EVER as adverb: at any time (past or future); at all times / always / continually; forever, eternally, to perpetuity (with a looser sense of an indefinite period, as the servant in Exodus 21:6); ever and anon; in any degree; a word of emphasis; and in composition, always or to eternity. His own biblical illustrations include Ephesians 5:29, Psalm 111, 2 Timothy 3:7, Exodus 3:15, and forever and ever. This page fills the KJV-gap adverb of duration. Companion pages already treat eternal, forever, and everlasting.
biblical_def: Ever in Scripture is not a mood and not a brand. It names the duration of God’s name, the stability of Christ, and the counterfeit of endless study without truth. The psalmist will not let covenant be seasonal: he will ever be mindful of his covenant (Psa 111:5). The apostle will not let learning be a virtue by itself: Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3:7). The church will not get a new Jesus by decade: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Heb 13:8). The throne will not be leased: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever (Psa 45:6). The house of the LORD is not a weekend: I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever (Psa 23:6). The dictionary therefore keeps ever from becoming either open-ended process or a slogan for self-help permanence. It is the Bible’s way of saying: always — as the Lord is, not as the age feels.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EVER as at any time; at all times / always; forever / to perpetuity (sometimes loosely, for an indefinite period); ever and anon; in any degree; and as a word of emphasis. He illustrates from Ephesians 5:29, Psalm 111, 2 Timothy 3:7, and Exodus 3:15.
webster_full: EV'ER, adverb At any time; at any period or point of time, past or future. Have you ever seen the city of Paris, or shall you ever see it?
No man ever yet hated his own flesh. Ephesians 5:29.
1. At all times; always; continually.
He will ever be mindful of his covenant. Psalms 111:5.
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. 2 Timothy 3:7.
2. Forever, eternally; to perpetuity; during everlasting continuance.
This is my name forever. Exodus 3:15.
In a more lax sense, this word signifies continually, for an indefinite period.
His master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall serve him forever. Exodus 21:6.
These words are sometimes repeated, for the sake of emphasis; forever and ever or forever and forever.
3. ever and anon, at one time and another; now and then.
4. In any degree. No man is ever the richer or happier for injustice.
Ever in composition signifies always or continually, without intermission, or to eternity.
scriptures: Psalm 111:5
He hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant.
2 Timothy 3:7
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
Hebrews 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
Psalm 45:6
Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.
Psalm 23:6
Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
corruption_summary: Ever is corrupted when the throne is treated as temporary, when ever learning is baptized as humility, and when for ever is emptied into a feeling of permanence without the living Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is process-God. Psalm 45:6 is for ever and ever; Hebrews 13:8 is the same Christ yesterday, today, and for ever. Open theism and every reduced Jesus keep the adverb and drop the throne. The recovery is the unchangeable Son, not a deity still becoming.

The second corruption is 2 Timothy 3:7 as a compliment. Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth is indictment. Credential culture and endless deconstruction treat non-arrival as sophistication. The dictionary will not. Learning that will not come to the truth is not humility; it is unbelief with a library card.

The third corruption is forever-as-brand. Therapeutic religion hears Psalm 23:6 as a spa: dwell in a mood for ever. The line is the house of the LORD, and Psalm 111:5 is a God who is ever mindful of His covenant. Permanence belongs to the Name, not to the self.
roots_summary: Webster: at any time / always / forever. Exodus 3:15 carries no Strong’s tag on ever in this cache; this page does not mint one.
roots_lines: Hebrew olam (H5769) — ever, everlasting (Psa 111:5; Psa 45:6 first ever); Hebrew ad (H5703) — perpetuity (Psa 45:6 second ever).
Hebrew orek (H753) — length (Psa 23:6, for ever as length, not a minted olam on that line).
Greek pantote (G3842) — ever, at all times (2 Tim 3:7); Greek aion (G165) — age, forever (Heb 13:8).
Exodus 3:15 is KJV-verified as Webster’s illustration (this is my name for ever); the cache does not tag ever with a Hebrew number on that verse line. No lemma is invented here.
usage: The LORD is ever mindful of His covenant (Psa 111:5); His throne is for ever and ever (Psa 45:6).
Ever learning without the truth is not humility (2 Tim 3:7).
Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever (Heb 13:8); the saint dwells in the house of the LORD for ever (Psa 23:6).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats SIDE as noun from Latin latus: the broad part of a surface; margin / verge; the part of an animal between back and belly; the slope of a hill; any part considered by direction; party / faction / sect; interest / favor (The LORD is on my side, Psalm 118:6); opposition; a branch of a family; quarter / region. As adjective: lateral, oblique. As verb: to lean; to embrace the opinions of a party. This page fills the KJV-gap word of place and allegiance. Companion pages already treat lord, blood, and neighbor.
biblical_def: Side in Scripture is not a team color and not a personality. It names the place of a body, the place of a neighbor, and the allegiance that will not stay neutral. Moses will not let the camp keep a third option: Who is on the LORD'S side? let him come unto me (Exo 32:26). The psalmist will not let fear write the roster: The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me? (Psa 118:6). The Gospel will not let the cross be a metaphor only: one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water (John 19:34). Protection is not a theory: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee (Psa 91:7). The priest is not excused by liturgy: when he saw him, he passed by on the other side (Luke 10:31). The dictionary therefore keeps side from becoming either partisan branding or a body without blood. It is the Bible’s way of saying: here, not there — and whose you are.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SIDE as the broad part or margin of a thing; the flank of a body; a slope; a party or faction; interest and favor (Psalm 118:6); and as a verb, to take a party. To take sides is to attach oneself to one interest against another.
webster_full: SIDE, noun [Latin latus.]
1. The broad and long part or surface of a thing, as distinguished from the end.
2. Margin; edge; verge; border; as the side of a river or a road.
3. The part of an animal between the back and the face and belly; the part of which the ribs are situated; as the right side; the left side.
4. The slope, declivity or ascent, as of a hill or mountain.
7. Party; faction; sect; any man or body of men considered as in opposition to another.
8. Interest; favor. The LORD is on my side. Psalm 118:6.
9. Any part being in opposition or contradistinction to another; in the battle, the slaughter was great on both sides.
To take sides, to embrace the opinions or attach one's self to the interest of a party when in opposition to another.
SIDE, verb intransitive. To embrace the opinions of one party or engage in its interest, when opposed to another party.
scriptures: Exodus 32:26
Then Moses stood in the gate of the camp, and said, Who is on the LORD'S side? let him come unto me. And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together unto him.
Psalm 118:6
The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?
John 19:34
But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water.
Psalm 91:7
A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.
Luke 10:31
And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
corruption_summary: Side is corrupted when the LORD’s side is recast as a party, when the pierced side is emptied of blood, and when the other side is how the religious pass by a neighbor.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Exodus 32:26 as a caucus. Who is on the LORD'S side? is not a campaign slogan. Partisan religion baptizes a faction and calls it Levi. The recovery is the Name, not the jersey. Psalm 118:6 remains The LORD is on my side — not the other way around as a mascot.

The second corruption is John 19:34 as art. The spear, the side, the blood and water are history. Liberal Protestant talk keeps the wound as a symbol of solidarity and drops the atonement. The dictionary will not. The side was pierced. The blood came out.

The third corruption is Luke 10:31 as professionalism. The priest passed by on the other side. Busy religion, liturgical religion, and online religion all know the move: keep clean, keep moving, keep the neighbor theoretical. Mercy is not a side-quest. It is obedience on this road.
roots_summary: Webster: flank / margin / party / favor. Exodus 32:26 and Psalm 118:6 carry no Strong’s tag on side in this cache; this page does not mint one.

usage: Moses asks, Who is on the LORD'S side? (Exo 32:26); the psalmist answers, The LORD is on my side (Psa 118:6).
Christ’s side was pierced; blood and water came out (John 19:34).
A thousand may fall at thy side (Psa 91:7); the priest who will not be a neighbor passes by on the other side (Luke 10:31).
